newsitem.title: USA: OPTIONS- March T-bonds see big trades pre-payrolls.
newsitem.headline: OPTIONS- March T-bonds see big trades pre-payrolls.

text.p: Big trades in the March contract, which have high-gamma implications because of its short maturity, dominated activity in U.S. Treasury bond options ahead of Friday's January jobs data, dealers said.

"Bonds have been relatively quiet, but in options, there have been a lot of big trades," said a brokerage trader at the Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT). "It's gamma (trade) because it's mostly in March and there hasn't been much in June."
Besides the big volatility plays, there was also a healthy flow of position-adjustment and hedging activities using short-dated options, he added.

High-gamma positions, typically achieved by buying short-dated options, are often deployed ahead of a major event to capture big swings in the underlying market. A negative gamma position aims to benefit from steep time-decay and post-event premium deflation associated with such options.
CBOT March T-bond futures options expire on February 21.

Early in the day, an investment bank bought 12,000 contracts of March 109 puts, traders said. Another firm sold 2,000 each of March 113 and 114 calls, while a third firm bought 5,000 of March 110 puts and a fourth firm sold 4,000 of March 109 puts.
Implied volatility for the March contract was off slightly at around 13.3 percent in late trade.

Although the market appeared fairly nervous ahead of the jobs data, traders said there seemed to be some sense of relief after the Federal Open Market Committee earlier in the week did not raise interest rates.
They added that growing expectation that the Federal Reserve would remain on hold for a while longer was part of the reason volatilities were at historically low levels.
June options, which still have about 100 days to expiry, lost a few tenths of a point to 9.9 percent.

Should the employment report be market-friendly, traders said volatilities could be further depressed, with the weekend time-decay adding pressure. Economists polled by Reuters have, on average, forecast a rise of 237,000 in January non-farm payrolls against a December gain of 262,000.

Option activity at the shorter end of the curve was quiet today, with implied volatility for June and September Eurodollar futures options largely unchanged at around 10.4 and 13.6 percent. There were a number of 1,000-lot deals but no multi-thousand-contract trades like those in bonds, a bank trader at the Chicago Mercantile Exchange said.
